Science.title: Canine cancer patients contribute to next-generation minimally invasive cancer therapies for dogs and humans
Science.summary: Natural disasters. Hikes. Long, dark nights alone. For many people, dogs offer a sense of safety and comfort in challenging or uncertain times. Cancer researchers at a new lab at Purdue University are partnering with dogs to make cancer less frightening—and less deadly—to some of humanity's very best friends using a technique called tumor ablation.

Science.title: Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet
Science.summary: The melting of the poles is increasingly shifting Earth's shape at a faster rate, with the planet becoming more and more round.

Science.title: Light-activated catalyst makes sustainable production of hydrogen peroxide more efficient
Science.summary: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is a versatile chemical feedstock whose industrial production relies predominantly on an energy-intensive process with a substantial environmental footprint. One alternative is to produce it using a catalyst activated by light. In an international research project involving the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces, researchers have now developed a synthesis strategy that allows them to precisely control the spatial arrangement of ions in a carbon nitride. The resulting photocatalyst is three times as efficient as conventional green production methods. The fi

Science.title: With climate-resilient crops in mind, study tackles flaw in photosynthesis
Science.summary: Rising temperatures and increasing drought are shortening crop-growing seasons in many parts of the world. Now scientists in Sweden report new advances toward engineering more efficient photosynthesis, work that could eventually contribute to efforts to adapt crops for climate change.

Science.title: Researchers develop AI tool to map microRNA binding sites on circular RNAs
Science.summary: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are loop-shaped molecules that can influence gene regulation through interactions with microRNAs (miRNAs). This matters because circRNAs can exist as different full-length isoforms, and their back-splice junction (BSJ) connects the two ends of the RNA. Treating a circular RNA like a linear transcript can therefore overlook sequence information near this junction.

Science.title: Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
Science.summary: Plants can't easily pick up and move when environmental conditions get rough, so they've evolved strategies to weather harsh conditions in place. That could help some plants survive in the face of a warming climate.

Science.title: Acupuncture and mutual exchange in Chinese and Soviet science
Science.summary: Previous accounts of the scientific relationship between communist China and the Soviet Union have depicted it as one of subordination, with the Russians exporting knowledge to the Chinese or scavenging from their bodies of knowledge. A new article in Isis, however, posits that the relationship between Chinese and Soviet scientists was instead one of mutual exchange. Science.title: How farming helped cause two medieval tsunamis in an Italian lake—and why the danger has returned
Science.summary: On Jan. 3, 1117, a strong earthquake shook northern Italy. A manuscript of the 12th century, kept today in the Vatican Library, recorded what came next: "The lakes also rose so much that very few of those living in the villages nearby escaped this danger."

Science.title: Stream restoration improves biodiversity but not necessarily ecosystem functioning
Science.summary: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation adopted in 2024 establishes the restoration of ecosystem functions as an objective of stream restoration. But can conventional measures that focus primarily on restoring the physical structure of rivers and streams fulfill this task?

Science.title: Surprising new pattern of groundwater loss may signal a turning point for the Colorado River Basin
Science.summary: During an intense drought from 2020 to 2022, the Upper Colorado River Basin lost far more groundwater than the Lower Basin did, despite having much higher natural recharge.

Science.title: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test
Science.summary: The full-scale prototype of Europe's Space Rider orbiter failed to deploy its parachute during a drop test earlier this month, but ESA officials hope the setback won't delay progress toward its first reusable spacecraft.

Science.title: Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03389-1 As machines race ahead in solving problems, mathematicians must establish a new era that prizes human understanding over simply publishing more solutions.

Science.title: Researcher tackles impact of a CMO's life events on businesses' bottom line
Science.summary: When a major company's CEO goes through a messy divorce or is arrested for drunk driving, investors often get nervous, worried that the executive's personal struggles will dent their returns. But most people hardly notice when a chief marketing officer has similar personal problems.

Science.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission
Science.summary: Victor Glover recalls how a suspected cabin leak warning came just 15 minutes before a crucial engine burn — and why receiving it just five minutes later could have changed everything.

Science.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.

Science.title: Microplastics in sediment could trace decades of human activity worldwide
Science.summary: In a review article recently published in the journal Earth-Science Reviews, researchers from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW), in collaboration with colleagues from the University of Leicester (United Kingdom), report on how human activity has altered Earth's sediments over the decades.

Science.title: James Webb telescope discovers surprising trove of metals around the Milky Way's supermassive black hole
Science.summary: New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope reveal a concentration of heavy metals near the Milky Way's central black hole. The discovery deepens a mystery about why our black hole behaves the way it does.

Science.title: DNA and underwater footage reveal two new species of deep-sea siphonophores
Science.summary: New research is shedding light on the diversity of deep-sea siphonophores. A team of scientists from MBARI, the University of Gdańsk, New York University and Yale University conducted a comprehensive examination of Bargmannia siphonophores using museum material, submersible observations and genomic sequencing. This work uncovered two previously unknown species: Bargmannia marlena and Bargmannia pyrosa. The team published their findings in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society last week.

Science.title: A rock plunged 90 kilometers into Earth and revealed something unexpected
Science.summary: Scientists discovered a rock in Papua New Guinea that plunged more than 90 kilometers beneath Earth's surface, revealing a bizarre temperature pattern that challenges established theories of Earth's interior. The unexpected shift from unusually hot to relatively cold conditions could transform our understanding of tectonic plate movements, earthquakes, and volcanoes.

Science.title: Natural forest regeneration helps curb spread of invasive species
Science.summary: The presence of non-native trees is often seen as an obstacle to the recovery of tropical forests regrowing in previously deforested areas. To better understand the behavior of these plants over time in both humid and dry forests, researchers from approximately 60 institutions analyzed data from over 1,500 areas of forest regeneration across the Americas. The results, published in the journal Nature Plants, indicate that the initial dominance of exotic species is temporary. Science.title: Revamped playground design could protect children around the world from dangers of the sun
Science.summary: A new design methodology for school playgrounds is demonstrating how children can still enjoy their playtime while being protected from the harmful effects of the sun.

Science.title: Brain scans reveal 'number line' that's used to mentally compare values
Science.summary: Although whole numbers and fractions are processed differently in the brain, when you compare their values, a single "mental map" akin to a number line lights up.

Science.title: Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03357-9 Analysis of nearly 30,000 brain scans yields detailed timeline of how the brain matures — and hints at the consequences of disrupting it.

Science.title: A house ages alongside its occupants, according to researcher
Science.summary: Flemish people are very attached to their homes and generally wish to stay there for as long as possible. However, many homes were not designed to be lived in for a lifetime. Architect and researcher Sander Lambrix has analyzed the relationship between our homes and our well-being as we grow older. His conclusion: a home is much more than just a physical environment, whether or not it is suited to an aging body. People and their homes are deeply connected on an emotional level.

Science.title: Disiplinang walang palo: Challenging common Filipino parenting misbeliefs
Science.summary: More frequent spanking is linked to greater anxiety and aggression in children over time, according to international research that includes Filipino families presented by psychology professor Dr. Liane Peña Alampay of the Ateneo de Manila University. The findings challenge the familiar belief that "pamamalo" produces more disciplined children, pointing instead to the benefits of warm relationships in the home, clear expectations and nonviolent disciplining.

Science.title: Supramolecular assembly opens a new route to building quantum materials
Science.summary: A joint research team fabricated a two-dimensional structure that exhibits properties of both the honeycomb and Kagome lattices using organic molecules. They discovered that edge states specific to topological materials (states that exist only at the edges and are distinct from those in the interior) appear in this structure. The team included researchers from NIMS, Toyota Kosen (National Institute of Technology, Toyota College), Saga University, Nara Women's University, Kiel University (Germany) and other institutions.

Science.title: Ants break a basic rule of biology to help them adapt to new environments
Science.summary: A new study led by researchers in the Eco-Evo-Devo lab at the University of Ottawa finds that ants can decouple antenna size from both head and body size as they develop into different social castes, revealing how social signals and hormones help shape traits for specialized colony roles.

Science.title: A parasite carried by one-third of humanity can't reproduce if one key protein is disabled
Science.summary: A protein discovered in a Virginia Tech–led study may open a gateway to treatments for a parasite responsible for a deadly disease in immunocompromised people. The team led by Raj Gaji, assistant professor of parasitology at the Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine working in the Center for One Health Research, identified a protein the team named DDP that helps Toxoplasma gondii build its offspring. When researchers switched it off, the parasites stopped multiplying entirely.

Science.title: Ultrafast light pulses track molecular motion with three-femtosecond resolution
Science.summary: Researchers have observed a molecule in the first instants after it has absorbed light and tracked the coordinated motion of electrons and nuclei with a temporal resolution of three femtoseconds. This is the result achieved by an international research group led by the Politecnico di Milano, which has developed a new apparatus for studying ultrafast photochemical processes.

Science.title: Amino acid stabilizes material's quantum state above room temperature
Science.summary: New research started with a special material that behaves unusually when it's extremely cold—135 degrees below zero Fahrenheit (minus 93 degrees Celsius), close to the most frigid temperature ever recorded in Antarctica—and showed that the unusual behavior could be extended to well above room temperature—up to about 135 F (57 degrees Celsius), close to the highest heat ever measured in Death Valley, California.

Science.title: Honey bees are bullying other bees, scientists discover
Science.summary: Honeybees are aggressively pushing wild pollinators away from flowers, with scientists documenting how they chase off rivals and dominate valuable food sources. New research warns that rising temperatures and increasing honeybee populations could intensify this competition, threatening wild bees and other important pollinators.

Science.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.

Science.title: Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery
Science.summary: An experiment has produced nanoflares similar to those seen on the sun, and shown that they can help explain why the outer layers of the solar atmosphere are so hot

Science.title: Material substitution can increase the potential environmental impact of packaging systems
Science.summary: New research suggests that replacing polyethylene (PE) packaging with paper, glass, aluminum or steel often does not reduce environmental impacts across a product's life cycle.

Science.title: The 2027 total solar eclipse will plunge these 10 ancient Egyptian temples and monuments into darkness
Science.summary: The "eclipse of the century" will plunge some of ancient Egypt's most spectacular sites into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027. These temples, tombs and monuments are inside the path of totality.

Science.title: A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
Science.summary: Researchers have developed a revolutionary microscope that uses an incredibly powerful laser to make previously invisible cellular structures easier to see. The technology dramatically improves image clarity, allowing scientists to examine small proteins that conventional electron microscopes struggle to capture. It could eventually reveal how tiny molecular machines interact inside cells, providing an unprecedented look at the hidden workings of life.

Science.title: Watch bizarre snake 'cartwheel' away from danger at more than 12 feet per second
Science.summary: Researchers filmed dwarf reed snakes ( Pseudorabdion ) from different angles to better understand how the serpents pull off their remarkable rolling behavior.

Science.title: Public health programs can 'rewire' social networks, study finds
Science.summary: An educational program intended to improve maternal and child health fundamentally altered the social fabric of the rural Honduran villages where it was implemented, a new Yale-led study finds. The findings, researchers say, have implications for interventions anywhere that seek to improve people's well-being by disseminating information or changing behaviors through social contagion.

Science.title: Crows may make lightning-fast decisions, sometimes twice as fast as humans, study hints
Science.summary: Carrion crows made decisions about their visual environments significantly faster than humans and primates tend to, according to a comparison in a new study.

Science.title: The great moth revival: how bogongs have bounced back
Science.summary: This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink If you live anywhere on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong moths are back in a big way . While we don’t yet have figures from ecologist-led surveys to compare with previous years, there is a wealth of data on the great moth revival being generated by citizen scientists across the eastern states. Continue reading...

Science.title: Shrinking iron films strengthens laser-driven demagnetization
Science.summary: From photos and videos to documents, vast amounts of data are stored on hard drives in large data centers. These devices use tiny magnetic regions whose orientation determines the information stored. But how could data be stored even faster in the future? One possible approach involves ultrashort laser pulses, which can alter the magnetic order of materials in an extremely short time.

Science.title: Helping microgreens pack even more of a nutritional punch
Science.summary: Microgreens are nutritional powerhouses. A team of plant scientists at Penn State conducting research on multiple aspects of microgreens recently published three studies reporting progress on multiple fronts, including iron enrichment, productive indoor growth and a faux lightning technique that could improve microgreens' growth, yield and nutritional quality.

Science.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
Science.summary: The new open-source model speaks the language of DNA and can help researchers understand the effects of any changes on gene activity and health.

Science.title: Extremely rare Viking Age coin from the reign of 'Olaf the Holy' may have been 'held in the king's own hand'
Science.summary: A massive Viking Age hoard that was discovered in Norway contains a rare silver coin featuring "Olaf the Holy," one of the country's first Christian kings.

Science.title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance

Science.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
Science.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.

Science.title: Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03414-3 From underwater speakers to growing super-corals, scientists battle to save reefs around the world.
